# China Unicom bets on AI cloud services to break telecoms revenue ceiling

Leveraging its formidable network and computing power, China Unicom is making cloud and AI services the cornerstone of its strategy to reshape its business value and secure a more central role in the digital ecosystem.

[![Picture of Jay Ian Birbeck](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt3d4d54955bda84c0/blt81b425b9b3309062/6511859b98d04b50e91c053c/default-contributor.png?width=100&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "Picture of Jay Ian Birbeck")](/author/jay-ian-birbeck)

[Jay Ian Birbeck](/author/jay-ian-birbeck)

March 27, 2026

4 Min Read

![](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt3d4d54955bda84c0/blt24c471496bcc7445/69c5663c3a4727cd0f7ebb30/China_Unicom_Poster.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&format=jpg&disable=upscale)

SOURCE: China Unicom

[China Unicom](https://www.cuguplus.com/home) is accelerating plans to deploy artificial intelligence across its consumer, enterprise and home services in 2026, as the country's third-largest wireless carrier looks to diversify its revenue streams beyond basic connectivity.

The push centers on cloud-based AI services that the carrier believes can open new revenue streams and further expand its market presence.

"Traditional communication services based on voice and data have already reached a ceiling in terms of revenue," said Chen Fengwei, deputy general manager of [Unicom Vsens Telecommunications](https://www.mwcshanghai.com/exhibitors/33296-unicom-vsens-telecommunications-co-ltd), speaking to Telecoms.com at Mobile World Congress. "Cloud and AI services built on top of communications will be a key opportunity for the future development of carriers."

The flagship product underpinning that strategy is China Unicom's [AI Cloud Phone,](https://www.huawei.com/en/news/2026/3/mwc-unicom-ai-reshaping) built in collaboration with Huawei and other partners, which runs a smartphone's operating system, applications and data on the carrier's own cloud servers rather than on a physical handset.

Related:[Yaqoot by Zain KSA Collaborates with Huawei](/partner-content/yaqoot-by-zain-ksa-partners-with-huawei-to-strengthen-business-support-systems)

Users access the virtual device remotely over Unicom's network, allowing a cheap handset to run apps and services that would normally require expensive hardware.

The service has signed up 18 million users to date. That is a fraction of Unicom's 450 million total mobile and broadband subscribers, but Chen described it as a foundation for far broader adoption.

"We believe that over the next few years, all of these 450 million users will fully adopt AI," he said.

The ambitions Chen outlined reflect a deeper strategic thinking among telecoms executives regarding industry value distribution: having built the infrastructure underpinning the digital economy, carriers now expect to play a much more central role in value creation within the digital ecosystem.

"Since the 3G era, carriers have been reduced to pipes while internet companies took center stage," Chen said. "Now, in the AI era, carriers have real strengths in computing power, data and AI, and they should use them."

To illustrate how, Chen pointed to Unicom's AI New Calling service, which embeds real-time translation and automated task execution directly into standard phone calls.

He offered two examples of how it could be used: a user opting in to real-time interpretation on a call with a foreign contact, or an AI agent completing a money transfer mid-call after the user mentions it out loud.

"In the past, you had to finish the call, open an app, and make the payment separately," Chen said. With AI agents embedded in the call, that sequence collapses into a single step. "This is something only carriers can do. App developers and device makers cannot."

Related:[AI Won't Fix Telecoms from the Sidelines, Analysts Warn](/partner-content/ai-won-t-fix-telecoms-from-the-sidelines-analysts-warn)

None of it works without the network underneath. Chen was direct on that point: the AI services Unicom is building depend on the kind of high-speed, low-latency connectivity that only the latest mobile and fiber infrastructure can provide.

Working alongside partners like Huawei, the carrier has upgraded more than 300 Chinese cities to 5G-A, which substantially increases upload speeds, a critical factor as AI applications constantly send data to the cloud for processing.

At MWC, Unicom also unveiled a combined AI and ultra-broadband connectivity package, aligning with a Chinese government strategy promoting 10-gigabit mobile and 1-gigabit fixed-line networks.

Unicom is also targeting the home as a growth market through a device called [Tone.](https://omdia.tech.informa.com/-/media/tech/omdia/marketing/commissioned-research/pdfs/china-unicom-and-huawei-revolutionizing-ai-agents.pdf?rev=5411f802781b4516ad16e9e91231458f) The small camera-equipped box acts as a household AI agent, routing media across screens, managing home network quality and responding to voice commands.

Chen said the device points to a broader shift in which cloud-connected computers could eventually replace home PCs, potentially sitting alongside fiber routers as the hub of home applications. Furthermore, China Unicom is collaborating with partners including Huawei to build a unified AI agent service platform. By integrating data across personal and home environments, the platform will enhance the capabilities of understanding user needs and cross-device collaboration—allowing AI to deliver highly personalized services tailored to each individual. 

Related:[AI helps China's cliff-dwelling primate pull back from extinction](/partner-content/ai-helps-china-s-cliff-dwelling-primate-pull-back-from-extinction)

He described a future of "generative and immersive" AI that works continuously in the background rather than waiting to be called on, with each user supported by dozens of specialized agents handling tasks simultaneously.

Setting the moment in a longer historical context, Chen compared the current AI transition to the 15-year build-out of the fixed internet and, later, the mobile internet.

"I now believe the future world will be one of AI, an age of native AI," Chen said. "2026 is just the starting point, and it will take a long time to truly make it a reality."
